claim: IL7RαhiCcr6+ lymphocytes in mouse LNs rapidly produce IL17 upon bacterial and fungal challenge.
source: Here, we report that IL7RhiCcr6+ lymphocytes in mouse LNs rapidly produce IL17 upon bacterial and fungal challenge.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing IL17 production 3 hours after challenge with heat-killed C. albicans, S. aureus bioparticles, and attenuated Y. pestis (Figure 1D).

claim: IL7RαhiCcr6+ innate-like lymphocytes are mostly LN resident.
source: We show that these innate-like lymphocytes are mostly LN resident.
evidence: Supported by photoconversion experiments showing ~75% of cells remained resident at 24 hours (Figure 2B) and parabiosis experiments showing limited exchange between paired mice (Figure 2C).

claim: Ccr6 is required for IL7RαhiCcr6+ lymphocyte accumulation near the SCS.
source: Ccr6 is required for their accumulation near the SCS and for efficient IL17 induction.
evidence: Supported by data showing reduced density of Ccr6-deficient cells near the SCS (Figure 4F) and reduced Thy1-PE labeling in Ccr6 KO mice (Figure 4G).

claim: Migration into the SCS intrinsically requires S1pr1.
source: Migration into the SCS intrinsically requires S1pr1, whereas movement from the sinus into the parenchyma involves the integrin LFA1 and its ligand ICAM1.
evidence: Supported by FTY720 treatment reducing Thy1-PE labeling (Figure 5C), S1pr1 deletion reducing CD169 association (Figure 5J,K), and imaging showing reduced SCS access after FTY720 (Figure 5L,M).

claim: Movement from the sinus into the parenchyma involves the integrin LFA1 and its ligand ICAM1.
source: Migration into the SCS intrinsically requires S1pr1, whereas movement from the sinus into the parenchyma involves the integrin LFA1 and its ligand ICAM1.
evidence: Supported by αL blocking antibody treatment causing increased Thy1-PE labeling (Figure 6D), reduced tracks crossing out of SCS (Figure 6K), and cells appearing stuck at the SCS floor (Figure 6I, Video 4).

claim: CD169 helps retain innate-like lymphocytes within the sinus, preventing their loss in lymph flow.
source: CD169, a sialic acid-binding lectin, helps retain the cells within the sinus, preventing their loss in lymph flow.
evidence: Supported by CD169 blockade causing loss of Vγ4+Ccr6+ cells from LN (Figure 7D), reduced Thy1-PE labeling after CD169 blockade (Figure 7E), and combined αL and CD169 blockade causing cell loss (Figure 7H).

claim: IL7RαhiCcr6+ lymphocytes include approximately 70% αβ T cells, 20% γδ T cells, and 5-10% non-T cells.
source: IL7RαhiCcr6+ innate-like lymphocytes within peripheral LNs express high amounts of Cxcr6 and they include ~70% αβ T cells, ~20% γδ T cells and 5–10% non-T cells (Figure 1A,B) (Gray et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by FACS analysis data shown in Figure 1B and cited previous work.

claim: IL7RαhiCcr6+ lymphocytes produce IL17 rapidly upon treatment with PMA and ionomycin or with IL1β and IL23.
source: Consistent with previous findings, the IL7RαhiCcr6+gd T cell subset produced IL17 rapidly upon treatment with phorbol 12-myristate 13-acetate (PMA) and ionomycin or with the cytokines IL1β and IL23 (Figure 1C, lower graph) (Cai et al., 2014; Gray et al., 2012; Gray et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by intracellular FACS data in Figure 1C and cited previous studies.

claim: IL7RαhiCcr6+ lymphocytes were the dominant IL17 producers at 3 hours after bacterial or fungal challenge.
source: IL7RαhiCcr6+ lymphocytes were the dominant IL17 producers at this early time point after challenge (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by FACS data showing IL17 production in IL7RαhiCcr6+ cells 3 hours after challenge with C. albicans, S. aureus, and Y. pestis (Figure 1D).

claim: Induction of IL17 expression in IL7RαhiCcr6+ cells upon bacterial challenge is dependent on CD169+ SCS macrophages.
source: The induction of IL17 expression in IL7RαhiCcr6+ cells upon bacterial challenge was dependent on CD169+ SCS macrophages as the response was greatly blunted in CD169-DTR mice (Miyake et al., 2007) pretreated with DT to ablate these cells (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by data showing reduced IL17 production in CD169-DTR mice after macrophage ablation (Figure 1E).

claim: Transcripts for Il1b and Il23a were upregulated after S. aureus bioparticle challenge.
source: Transcripts for both Il1b and Il23a were upregulated (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data showing increased mRNA levels (Figure 1F).

claim: Induction of IL17 following S. aureus bioparticle challenge is compromised in mice lacking the ASC inflammasome subunit.
source: Induction of IL17 following S. aureus bioparticle challenge was compromised in mice lacking the ASC (Apoptosis-associated speck-like protein containing a CARD) inflammasome subunit (Figure 1G), consistent with a role for IL1β in activating IL7RαhiCcr6+ cells during the response to these bacteria.
evidence: Supported by data showing reduced IL17 production in ASC-deficient mice (Figure 1G).

claim: IL7RαhiCcr6+ cells make up approximately 0.5% of peripheral LN cells but only 0.1% of cells in blood.
source: IL7RαhiCcr6+ lymphocytes make up ~0.5% of peripheral LN cells yet they represent only ~0.1% of cells in blood (Figure 2A), suggesting that the cells are largely non-recirculatory under homeostatic conditions.
evidence: Supported by FACS analysis data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: At 24 hours after photoconversion, almost three quarters of IL7RαhiCcr6+ cells remained resident in the LN.
source: At 24 hr after photoconversion almost three quarters of the IL7RαhiCcr6+ cells and a similar fraction of the Vγ4+Ccr6+ cells remained resident in the LN, whereas more than 80% of the conventional αβ T cells and Ccr6– Vγ4+ T cells had left the LN and been replaced by newly arriving cells.
evidence: Supported by photoconversion experiments in KikGR mice (Figure 2B).

claim: At 48 hours after photoconversion, the innate-like lymphocyte pool showed little further exchange, whereas naive αβ T cells were 90% replaced.
source: At 48 hr, the innate-like lymphocyte pool showed little further exchange, whereas naive αβ T cells were 90% replaced (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by photoconversion experiments in KikGR mice (Figure 2B).

claim: Two weeks following parabiosis surgery, the naive αβ T cell compartment achieved full chimerism, whereas innate-like lymphocytes showed only limited exchange.
source: Two weeks following surgery the naive αβ T cell compartment and the Ccr6– Vγ4+ T cells had achieved full chimerism, whereas the innate-like lymphocytes showed only limited exchange between the paired mice (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by parabiosis experiments (Figure 2C).

claim: Cxcr6GFP/+ cells frequently make contact with CD169+ macrophages and occasionally cross the layer of macrophages to reach the SCS.
source: A closer examination of Cxcr6GFP/+ cell behavior in this region revealed that the cells frequently made contact with CD169+ macrophages, and occasionally, lymphocytes could be observed crossing the layer of macrophages to reach the SCS (Figure 3A and Videos 1 and 2).
evidence: Supported by intravital two-photon microscopy observations (Figure 3A, Videos 1 and 2).

claim: Cells initially detected within the SCS can migrate across the CD169+ macrophage layer into the LN parenchyma.
source: Reciprocally, cells that were initially detected within the SCS could be observed migrating across the thick CD169+ macrophage layer into the LN parenchyma (Figure 3A and Videos 1 and 2).
evidence: Supported by intravital two-photon microscopy observations (Figure 3A, Videos 1 and 2).

claim: Approximately 25% of Cxcr6GFP/+ cell tracks within 50 µm of the capsule are in the SCS.
source: Among all the tracks of Cxcr6GFP/+ cells within 50 µm of the capsule, ~25% were in the SCS (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by quantitative cell tracking analysis (Figure 3B).

claim: About 3% of cells in the SCS region traveled from the parenchyma into the sinus, and 3% traveled in the reverse direction, in 30 min imaging periods.
source: Cell tracking analysis showed that about 3% of the cells in the SCS region traveled from the parenchyma into the sinus, and 3% of the cells traveled in the reverse direction, in the 30 min imaging periods (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by quantitative cell tracking analysis (Figure 3C).

claim: Approximately 10% of total IL7RαhiCcr6+ cells were brightly labeled with Thy1-PE antibody after footpad injection.
source: Approximately 10% of the total IL7RαhiCcr6+ cells were brightly labeled with Thy1-PE antibody compared with about 0.3% of naive T cells (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by in vivo Thy1-PE labeling experiments (Figure 3D).

claim: Among innate-like lymphocytes, γδ T cells (predominantly Vγ4+Ccr6+ cells) were preferentially labeled with Thy1-PE, with around 15-20% of these cells being antibody exposed.
source: Among the innate-like lymphocytes, γδ T cells (predominantly Vγ4+Ccr6+ cells) were preferentially labeled, with around 15–20% of these cells being antibody exposed.
evidence: Supported by in vivo Thy1-PE labeling experiments (Figure 3D).

claim: 30-40% of IL7RαhiCcr6+ innate-like lymphocytes isolated from control mice were CD169 macrophage-derived membrane bleb positive.
source: In accord with previous findings, 30–40% of the IL7RαhiCcr6+ innate-like lymphocytes isolated from control mice were CD169 macrophage-derived membrane bleb positive (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by FACS analysis data (Figure 3F) and cited previous findings.

claim: A higher frequency (40-55%) of Vγ4+γδ T cells were CD169 bleb positive, suggesting these cells may be preferentially associated with SCS macrophages.
source: A higher frequency (40–55%) of the Vγ4+γδ T cells were CD169 bleb positive, suggesting these cells may be preferentially associated with SCS macrophages (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by FACS analysis data (Figure 3F).

claim: Lymph-exposed innate-like lymphocytes, but not total αβ T cells, were enriched for CD169-bleb-positive cells.
source: Combining this analysis with Thy1-PE labeling showed that lymph-exposed innate-like lymphocytes, but not total αβ T cells, were enriched for CD169-bleb-positive cells (Figure 3G).
evidence: Supported by combined Thy1-PE labeling and CD169 staining analysis (Figure 3G).

claim: CCL20 is expressed in LN lymphatic endothelial cells at levels more than 100-fold higher than other LN lymphoid stromal cells.
source: Although CCL20 is not abundantly expressed in LNs, it is expressed in LN lymphatic endothelial cells (LECs) at levels more than 100-fold higher than other LN lymphoid stromal cells (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data showing Ccl20 mRNA abundance in sorted cell populations (Figure 4A).

claim: CCL20 protein is present in the subcapsular sinus region but not in the medullary sinus region.
source: Immunofluorescence microscopy showed evidence of CCL20 protein in the subcapsular sinus region (overlying follicular and interfollicular regions) but not in the medullary sinus region (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1) consistent with findings in primate LNs (Choi et al., 2003; Pegu et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1) and cited studies in primate LNs.

claim: Innate-like lymphocytes are responsive to CCL20 by in vitro migration assays.
source: Innate-like lymphocytes were responsive to CCL20 by in vitro migration assays (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by transwell migration assay data (Figure 4C).

claim: When CCL20 is injected subcutaneously, IL7RαhiCcr6+Cxcr6hi lymphocytes become clustered near and within the SCS in draining LNs.
source: When CCL20 was injected subcutaneously into Cxcr6GFP/+ mice, IL7RαhiCcr6+Cxcr6hi lymphocytes became clustered near and within the SCS in the draining LNs (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data after CCL20 injection (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).

claim: Cells from CCL20-injected LNs showed reduced surface Ccr6, increased CD169 staining, and increased Thy1 labeling.
source: Cells from these LNs showed reduced surface Ccr6, and increased CD169 staining and Thy1 labeling, consistent with their having been exposed to increased amounts of CCL20 and localizing near and within the SCS (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by FACS analysis data after CCL20 injection (Figure 4E).

claim: Ccr6-deficient cells are reduced in density near the SCS despite being slightly increased in total frequency in the LN.
source: We next examined the distribution of Ccr6-deficient (KO) cells in Ccr6GFP/GFP mice and found that the cells were reduced in density near the SCS (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 3) despite being slightly increased in total frequency in the LN (not shown).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data in Ccr6 KO mice (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 3).

claim: Ccr6 KO mice showed reduced frequencies of Thy1-PE labeled cells, most significantly for the Vγ4+ population.
source: In Thy1-PE labeling experiments, Ccr6 KO mice showed reduced frequencies of labeled cells, a result that was most significant for the Vγ4+ population (Figure 4G).
evidence: Supported by in vivo Thy1-PE labeling experiments in Ccr6 KO mice (Figure 4G).

claim: Ccr6-GFP+ IL7Rαhi cells and the Vγ4+ subset from Ccr6 KO mice were associated with less CD169+ blebs compared with Ccr6-sufficient controls.
source: Consistent with reduced proximity to SCS macrophages, Ccr6-GFP+ IL7Rαhi cells and the Vγ4+ subset from Ccr6 KO mice were associated with less CD169+ blebs compared with Ccr6-sufficient controls (Figure 4H).
evidence: Supported by CD169 bleb staining data in Ccr6 KO mice (Figure 4H).

claim: Vγ4+Ccr6+ T cells uniquely express the surface marker Scart2.
source: Vγ4+Ccr6+ T cells uniquely express the surface marker Scart2 (Figure 4I) (Gray et al., 2013; Kisielow et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by FACS analysis data (Figure 4I) and cited previous studies.

claim: Scart2 antibody treatment labeled fewer Vγ4+ cells in LNs from Ccr6-deficient mice than from wild-type mice.
source: In a complementary approach to Thy1 labeling, Scart2 antibody treatment was found to label fewer Vγ4+ cells in LNs from Ccr6-deficient mice than from wild-type mice (Figure 4I).
evidence: Supported by in vivo Scart2 antibody labeling experiments (Figure 4I).

claim: Scart2+ γδ T cells were underrepresented in the SCS region in LN sections from Ccr6-deficient mice compared with control mice.
source: By immunofluorescence microscopy, Scart2+ γδ T cells were underrepresented in the SCS region in LN sections from Ccr6-deficient mice compared with those from control mice (Figure 4J, Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data (Figure 4J, Figure 4—figure supplement 4).

claim: When Ccr6 KO mice were immunized with S. aureus bioparticles, the IL7RαhiCcr6+ cells mounted a diminished IL17 response.
source: Importantly, when Ccr6 KO mice were immunized with S. aureus bioparticles, the IL7RαhiCcr6+ cells mounted a diminished IL17 response (Figure 4K), whereas they responded normally to activation stimuli in vitro (not shown).
evidence: Supported by intracellular IL17 staining data after S. aureus challenge in Ccr6 KO mice (Figure 4K).

claim: Innate-like lymphocytes have detectable surface S1pr1.
source: The innate-like lymphocytes had detectable surface S1pr1 (Figure 5A) and they responded to S1P by in vitro migration in a Transwell assay (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by FACS analysis showing S1pr1 surface expression (Figure 5A).

claim: Innate-like lymphocytes respond to S1P by in vitro migration in a Transwell assay.
source: The innate-like lymphocytes had detectable surface S1pr1 (Figure 5A) and they responded to S1P by in vitro migration in a Transwell assay (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by transwell migration assay data (Figure 5B).

claim: Pretreatment of mice for 6 hr with FTY720 greatly diminished in vivo Thy1-PE labeling on IL7RαhiCcr6+ lymphocytes.
source: Pretreatment of mice for 6 hr with FTY720, a functional antagonist of S1pr1, greatly diminished in vivo Thy1-PE labeling on IL7RαhiCcr6+ lymphocytes (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by in vivo Thy1-PE labeling experiments after FTY720 treatment (Figure 5C).

claim: In vivo Scart2 antibody labeling of Vγ4+γδ T cells was decreased after FTY720 treatment.
source: Similarly, in vivo Scart2 antibody labeling of Vγ4+γδ T cells was decreased after FTY720 treatment (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by in vivo Scart2 labeling experiments after FTY720 treatment (Figure 5D).

claim: FTY720 decreased the CD169 membrane bleb positive fraction to 20-25% in both the total IL7RαhiCcr6+ population and the γδ T cell subpopulation.
source: FTY720 also decreased the CD169 membrane bleb positive fraction to 20–25% in both the total IL7RαhiCcr6+ population and the γδ T cell subpopulation (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by CD169 bleb staining data after FTY720 treatment (Figure 5C).

claim: Treatment with the selective S1pr1 functional antagonist AUY954 produced comparable findings to FTY720.
source: Comparable findings were made after treatment with the more selective S1pr1 functional antagonist, AUY954 (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by CD169 bleb staining data after AUY954 treatment (Figure 5E).

claim: FTY720 treatment caused a loss of Cxcr6GFP/+ cells from the SCS as shown by immunofluorescence microscopy.
source: Examination of tissue sections by immunofluorescence microscopy showed a loss of Cxcr6GFP/+ cells from the SCS following FTY720 treatment (Figure 5F).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data after FTY720 treatment (Figure 5F).

claim: FTY720 treatment caused a depletion of Scart2+ cells from the SCS.
source: FTY720 treatment also caused a depletion of Scart2+ cells from the SCS (Figure 5G, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data after FTY720 treatment (Figure 5G, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).

claim: In mice unable to produce lymphatic S1P, innate-like lymphocytes had less CD169+ macrophage-derived membrane blebs and less in vivo Thy1-PE antibody labeling.
source: In mice unable to produce lymphatic S1P due to generalized Sphk2 deficiency and ablation of Sphk1 in lymphatic endothelium, innate-like lymphocytes had less CD169+ macrophage-derived membrane blebs and less in vivo Thy1-PE antibody labeling compared with control mice (Figure 5H).
evidence: Supported by data from Lyve1-Cre Sphk1fl/-Sphk2-/- mice (Figure 5H).

claim: The macrophage-derived bleb coating is restricted to S1pr1+ cells.
source: In accord with S1pr1 having an intrinsic role in promoting SCS access of IL7RαhiCcr6+ cells, staining for S1pr1 and CD169 showed the macrophage-derived bleb coating was restricted to the S1pr1+ cells (Figure 5I).
evidence: Supported by combined S1pr1 and CD169 staining data (Figure 5I).

claim: Tamoxifen treatment of S1pr1f/f CreERt2+ mice for 5 days caused a loss of S1pr1 in innate-like lymphocytes.
source: Tamoxifen treatment of adult mice for 5 days caused a loss of S1pr1 in innate-like lymphocytes (Figure 5J).
evidence: Supported by FACS analysis after tamoxifen treatment (Figure 5J).

claim: Loss of S1pr1 was associated with reduced in vivo Thy1-PE labeling and reduced CD169 on IL7RαhiCcr6+ cells.
source: Analysis in separate mice showed that the loss of S1pr1 was associated with reduced in vivo Thy1-PE labeling and reduced CD169 on IL7RαhiCcr6+ cells (Figure 5J).
evidence: Supported by FACS analysis after tamoxifen-induced S1pr1 deletion (Figure 5J).

claim: Under conditions of partial S1pr1 ablation, S1pr1-deleted cells lost their CD169 association.
source: In another approach, mice were treated with tamoxifen for a short time to cause a ~50% reduction in the fraction of cells that were S1pr1+ (Figure 5K). We reasoned that if S1pr1 were acting cell intrinsically in IL7RαhiCcr6+ cells then under conditions of partial ablation the S1pr1-deleted cells should lose their CD169 association whereas this would not occur if the receptor were acting in another cell type. Consistent with an intrinsic role, there was little CD169 staining of S1pr1-negative cells in the tamoxifen-treated mice (Figure 5K).
evidence: Supported by FACS analysis after short-term tamoxifen treatment (Figure 5K).

claim: FTY720 treatment caused fewer Cxcr6GFP/+ innate-like lymphocytes to be present in the SCS.
source: Visual inspection of the imaging data for FTY720-treated versus control LNs suggested that there were fewer Cxcr6GFP/+ innate-like lymphocytes in the SCS after FTY720 treatment and less examples of cells migrating into the sinus (Video 3). Quantification of the number of tracks present in the SCS and the parenchyma in four imaging experiments confirmed that there were fewer cells in the sinus (Figure 5L), and there was a significant reduction in the number of tracks that crossed from the parenchyma into the sinus (Figure 5M).
evidence: Supported by intravital two-photon microscopy and quantitative cell tracking analysis (Figure 5L, M, Video 3).

claim: FTY720 caused a significant reduction in the number of tracks that crossed from the parenchyma into the sinus.
source: Quantification of the number of tracks present in the SCS and the parenchyma in four imaging experiments confirmed that there were fewer cells in the sinus (Figure 5L), and there was a significant reduction in the number of tracks that crossed from the parenchyma into the sinus (Figure 5M).
evidence: Supported by quantitative cell tracking analysis (Figure 5M).

claim: Innate-like lymphocytes express high levels of LFA1 (αLβ2) integrin.
source: Innate-like lymphocytes express high levels of LFA1 (αLβ2) integrin (Figure 6A) and ICAM1 is highly expressed by LECs lining the SCS (Cohen et al., 2014) (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by FACS analysis showing LFA1 expression (Figure 6A).

claim: ICAM1 is highly expressed by LECs lining the SCS.
source: Innate-like lymphocytes express high levels of LFA1 (αLβ2) integrin (Figure 6A) and ICAM1 is highly expressed by LECs lining the SCS (Cohen et al., 2014) (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data (Figure 6B) and cited previous study.

claim: ICAM1 is also expressed by CD169+ SCS macrophages.
source: ICAM1 is also expressed by CD169+ SCS macrophages (not shown).
evidence: Stated as an observation but data not shown.

claim: IL7RαhiCcr6+ cells bind avidly to ICAM1 in adhesion assays.
source: In adhesion assays, IL7RαhiCcr6+ cells bound avidly to ICAM1 (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by in vitro adhesion assay data (Figure 6C).

claim: The Vγ4+ subset had slightly lower LFA1 than the total IL7RαhiCcr6+ population and adhered less strongly to ICAM1.
source: The Vγ4+ subset had slightly lower LFA1 than the total IL7RαhiCcr6+ population and adhered less strongly to ICAM1 (Figure 6A,C).
evidence: Supported by FACS analysis and adhesion assay data (Figure 6A, C).

claim: 6-hr αL blocking antibody treatment caused increased Thy1-PE labeling on total IL7RαhiCcr6+ lymphocytes and on the Vγ4+γδ T cell subset.
source: Consistent with this model, 6-hr αL blocking antibody treatment caused increased Thy1-PE labeling on total IL7RαhiCcr6+ lymphocytes and on the Vγ4+γδ T cell subset, without influencing their total number in the LN (Figure 6D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by in vivo Thy1-PE labeling experiments after αL blockade (Figure 6D).

claim: A similar increase in the frequency of Thy1-PE labeled innate-like lymphocytes was observed in Icam1-/- mice compared to littermate controls.
source: A similar increase in the frequency of Thy1-PE labeled innate-like lymphocytes was observed in Icam1-/- mice compared to littermate controls (Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by in vivo Thy1-PE labeling experiments in ICAM1 KO mice (Figure 6E).

claim: Icam1-/- mice had less IL7RαhiCcr6+ and Vγ4+Ccr6+ cells compared with ICAM1 sufficient control mice.
source: However, Icam1-/- mice had less IL7RαhiCcr6+ and Vγ4+Ccr6+ cells compared with ICAM1 sufficient control mice, whereas the cells were present at an increased frequency in blood (Figure 6F,G).
evidence: Supported by FACS analysis in ICAM1 KO mice (Figure 6F, G).

claim: When mice were treated with αL blocking antibody for 3 days, there was a reduction in IL7RαhiCcr6+ cell number in LNs and a marked increase in their numbers in blood.
source: When mice were treated with αL blocking antibody for 3 days, there was a similar reduction in IL7RαhiCcr6+ cell number in LNs and a marked increase in their numbers in blood (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by FACS analysis after 3-day αL blockade (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).

claim: IL7Rαhi cells were enriched in the SCS in αL blocked mice by immunofluorescence microscopy.
source: By immunofluorescence microscopy, IL7Rαhi cells were found enriched in the SCS in αL blocked mice (Figure 6H).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data after αL blockade (Figure 6H).

claim: After αL blockade, many Cxcr6GFP/+ cells appeared to be 'stuck' to the SCS floor with their cell bodies 'fluttering' in the sinus.
source: Visual inspection of the movies revealed many Cxcr6GFP/+ cells that appeared to be 'stuck' to the SCS floor with their cell bodies 'fluttering' in the sinus, possibly being moved by passing lymph (Figure 6I and Video 4).
evidence: Supported by intravital two-photon microscopy observations (Figure 6I, Video 4).

claim: Cells stuck to the SCS floor after αL blockade had an elongated morphology compared to the rounded shape of cells in the SCS of control mice.
source: These cells had an elongated morphology compared to the rounded shape of cells in the SCS of control mice (Figure 6I and Video 4).
evidence: Supported by intravital two-photon microscopy observations and axis ratio measurements (Figure 6I, Video 4).

claim: αL treatment caused an increase of cells in the sinus in association with the macrophage layer.
source: Consistent with the in vivo Thy1-PE labeling and IF microscopy, quantitative analysis of the imaging experiments by enumerating cell tracks and by a computational approach revealed that αL treatment caused an increase of cells in the sinus in association with the macrophage layer (Figure 6J, Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by quantitative cell tracking analysis and computational analysis (Figure 6J, Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).

claim: Cell tracking analysis showed that while there was not a significant change in the frequency of tracks crossing from the parenchyma into the SCS after αL blockade, there was a significant reduction in cells traveling from the SCS into the parenchyma.
source: Moreover, the cell tracking analysis showed that while there was not a significant change in the frequency of tracks crossing from the parenchyma into the SCS, there was a significant reduction in cells traveling from the SCS into the parenchyma (Figure 6K).
evidence: Supported by quantitative cell tracking analysis (Figure 6K).

claim: IL7RαhiCcr6+ lymphocytes have a high amount of CD169 ligand on their surface.
source: By CD169-Fc staining, we found IL7RαhiCcr6+ lymphocytes had a high amount of CD169 ligand on their surface, and neuraminidase treatment of the cells abolished their ability to bind CD169 (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by CD169-Fc binding assay data (Figure 7A).

claim: Neuraminidase treatment of IL7RαhiCcr6+ lymphocytes abolished their ability to bind CD169.
source: By CD169-Fc staining, we found IL7RαhiCcr6+ lymphocytes had a high amount of CD169 ligand on their surface, and neuraminidase treatment of the cells abolished their ability to bind CD169 (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by CD169-Fc binding assay data after neuraminidase treatment (Figure 7A).

claim: The acquisition of abundant macrophage membrane fragments by innate-like lymphocytes is dependent on CD169.
source: The acquisition of abundant macrophage membrane fragments by innate-like lymphocytes was dependent on CD169, since in mice in which CD169 was blocked with a neutralizing antibody (Crocker and Gordon, 1989) or in mice deficient in CD169, there were no CD11b+ macrophage membrane fragments on innate-like lymphocytes (Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by FACS analysis in CD169-blocked or CD169-deficient mice (Figure 7B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).

claim: CD169 blockade in Cxcr6GFP/+ mice appeared to increase the amount of innate-like lymphocyte migration within the SCS and between parenchyma and sinus.
source: By real-time two photon microscopy, CD169 blockade in Cxcr6GFP/+ mice appeared to increase the amount of innate-like lymphocyte migration within the SCS and between parenchyma and sinus (Video 5). Quantitation of the cell tracks crossing between compartments confirmed that there was an increase in bidirectional exchange (Figure 7C).
evidence: Supported by intravital two-photon microscopy and quantitative cell tracking analysis (Figure 7C, Video 5).

claim: After 30 hr of treatment with CD169-blocking antibody, there was a two-fold loss of Vγ4+Ccr6+ cells in the LN.
source: After 30 hr of treatment with CD169-blocking antibody, there was no change in total IL7RαhiCcr6+ cell frequency, but there was a two-fold loss of Vγ4+Ccr6+ cells in the LN (Figure 7D).
evidence: Supported by FACS analysis after 30-hr CD169 blockade (Figure 7D).

claim: In 6-hr CD169 blockade experiments, there was a significant reduction in the fraction of Vγ4+Ccr6+ cells that were Thy1-PE labeled.
source: Indeed, in 6-hr blockade experiments, there was a significant reduction in the fraction of Vγ4+Ccr6+ cells that were Thy1-PE labeled (Figure 7E).
evidence: Supported by in vivo Thy1-PE labeling experiments after 6-hr CD169 blockade (Figure 7E).

claim: A loss of Vγ4+Ccr6+ cells was observed following CD169+ macrophage ablation using CD169-DTR mice.
source: A loss of Vγ4+Ccr6+ cells was also observed following CD169+ macrophage ablation using CD169-DTR mice (Figure 7F).
evidence: Supported by FACS analysis after macrophage ablation in CD169-DTR mice (Figure 7F).

claim: In ICAM1 adhesion assays, Vγ4+Ccr6+ cells were less capable of binding ICAM1 compared with other innate-like lymphocytes.
source: In considering explanations for why these effects were mostly selective to the Vγ4+Ccr6+ subpopulation, we found it notable that in ICAM1 adhesion assays, Vγ4+Ccr6+ cells were less capable of binding ICAM1 compared with other innate-like lymphocytes (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by in vitro adhesion assay data (Figure 6C).

claim: Within 2 hr of anti-CD169 treatment following αL blockade, enhanced Thy1 labeling was lost, indicating loss of innate-like lymphocytes from the sinus.
source: In the first 4 hr following αL treatment, we observed a gradual increase in the fraction of cells that were Thy1-PE+ (Figure 7G), consistent with the accumulation of cells in the sinus (Figure 6). Within 2 hr of anti-CD169 treatment, this enhanced Thy1 labeling was lost, indicating loss of innate-like lymphocytes from the sinus, and there was a reduction in IL7RαhiCcr6+ cell frequency (Figure 7G).
evidence: Supported by time-course experiments with combined αL and CD169 blockade (Figure 7G).

claim: When αL and CD169 were both blocked continually for 6 hr, there was a 50% loss of total innate-like lymphocytes in LNs, accompanied by an increase of the cells in blood.
source: When αL and CD169 were both blocked continually for 6 hr, there was a 50% loss of total innate-like lymphocytes in LNs, and this was accompanied by an increase of the cells in blood (Figure 7H).
evidence: Supported by FACS analysis after 6-hr combined αL and CD169 blockade (Figure 7H).

claim: After αL blocking antibody treatment, there was a loss of Thy1-PE labeling and in total IL7RαhiCcr6+ cells in CD169 KO mice compared with Het controls.
source: In CD169 Het and KO mice, there were comparable starting frequencies of IL7RαhiCcr6+ cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C), but after αL blocking antibody treatment there was a loss of Thy1-PE labeling and in total IL7RαhiCcr6+ cells in the CD169 KO mice compared with the Het controls (Figure 7I).
evidence: Supported by FACS analysis after αL blockade in CD169 KO mice (Figure 7I).

claim: Unlike αL blockade which caused innate-like lymphocytes to become non-migratory and stuck to the SCS floor, applying anti-CD169 in addition to anti-αL led to innate-like lymphocyte detachment from CD169+ macrophages and loss in the lymph flow.
source: Importantly, unlike αL blockade, which caused many innate-like lymphocytes to become non-migratory and apparently stuck to the SCS floor (Video 4), applying anti-CD169 in addition to anti-αL led to innate-like lymphocyte detachment from CD169+ macrophages and loss in the lymph flow (Video 7).
evidence: Supported by intravital two-photon microscopy observations (Video 4, Video 7).

claim: Combined αL and anti-CD169 treatment caused a decrease of cells from the sinus region by quantitative analysis.
source: By quantitative analysis of three imaging experiments, CD169-blockade or deficiency was found to have little effect on the density of Cxcr6GFP/+ cells in the SCS, but combined αL and anti-CD169 treatment caused a decrease of cells from the sinus region (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of imaging experiments (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D, E).

claim: IL7RαhiCcr6+ lymphocytes show binding to plates coated with recombinant WT but not a binding site mutant of CD169 in adhesion assays.
source: In adhesion assays, IL7RαhiCcr6+ lymphocytes showed binding to plates coated with recombinant WT but not a binding site mutant of CD169 (Figure 7J).
evidence: Supported by in vitro adhesion assay data (Figure 7J).

claim: Naive αβ T cells showed minimal binding to CD169 in adhesion assays.
source: By contrast, naïve αβ T cells showed minimal binding to CD169 (Figure 7J).
evidence: Supported by in vitro adhesion assay data (Figure 7J).

claim: The Ccr6-dependent positioning of IL7RαhiCcr6+ innate-like lymphocytes near the LN SCS is important for their rapid cytokine production following bacterial or fungal challenge.
source: The above findings show that the Ccr6-dependent positioning of IL7RαhiCcr6+ innate-like lymphocytes near the LN SCS is important for their rapid cytokine production following bacterial or fungal challenge.
evidence: Supported by data showing reduced IL17 response in Ccr6 KO mice after S. aureus challenge (Figure 4K) and inference from positioning data.

claim: Lymphatic endothelial-derived CCL20 acts on Ccr6 to attract innate-like lymphocytes into proximity with SCS macrophages.
source: The data support a model (Figure 8) where lymphatic endothelial-derived CCL20 acts on Ccr6 to attract the innate-like lymphocytes into proximity with SCS macrophages.
evidence: Supported by data showing CCL20 expression in LECs (Figure 4A), CCL20 protein in SCS region (Figure 4B), and reduced SCS proximity in Ccr6 KO mice (Figure 4F-J).

claim: Innate-like lymphocytes exchange between the LN parenchyma and the SCS.
source: Real time intravital two photon microscopy and in vivo labeling procedures revealed that innate-like lymphocytes exchanged between the LN parenchyma and the SCS.
evidence: Supported by intravital two-photon microscopy showing bidirectional cell movement (Figure 3A, Videos 1 and 2) and cell tracking analysis (Figure 3C).

claim: This requirement for CD169 in sinus retention was most prominent for the Vγ4+γδ T cell subset of innate-like lymphocytes.
source: This requirement was most prominent for the Vγ4+γδ T cell subset of innate-like lymphocytes.
evidence: Supported by data showing selective loss of Vγ4+Ccr6+ cells after CD169 blockade (Figure 7D, E) and their higher CD169 bleb coating (Figure 3F).

claim: IL17 is a cytokine with roles in anti-bacterial and anti-fungal defense that is made abundantly by effector T cells at epithelial surfaces.
source: IL17 is a cytokine with roles in anti-bacterial and anti-fungal defense that is made abundantly by effector T cells at epithelial surfaces (Littman and Rudensky, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to established knowledge in the field.

claim: CD169 is the founding member of the Siglec family of sialic acid-binding lectins.
source: CD169 is the founding member of the Siglec family of sialic acid-binding lectins (Crocker et al., 2007; Macauley et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to established knowledge in the field.

claim: IL17 is known to play a role in host defense against cutaneous Candida albicans and Staphyloccus aureus infection.
source: IL17 is known to play a role in host defense against cutaneous Candida albicans and Staphyloccus aureus infection (Cho et al., 2010; Conti and Gaffen, 2015) and to be induced in rats by Y. pestis (Comer et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: IL17 is induced in rats by Y. pestis.
source: IL17 is known to play a role in host defense against cutaneous Candida albicans and Staphyloccus aureus infection (Cho et al., 2010; Conti and Gaffen, 2015) and to be induced in rats by Y. pestis (Comer et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: S1P and S1pr1 have a critical role in promoting egress of T and B cells from LNs, acting at the step of transmigration into cortical and medullary sinuses.
source: S1P and S1pr1 have a critical role in promoting egress of T and B cells from LNs, acting at the step of transmigration into cortical and medullary sinuses (Grigorova et al., 2009; Sinha et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: S1pr1 is required for marginal zone (MZ) B cell shuttling between the S1P high MZ and the S1P low lymphoid follicle.
source: S1pr1 is also required for marginal zone (MZ) B cell shuttling between the S1P high MZ and the S1P low lymphoid follicle (Arnon et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: LFA1 and ICAM1 have well-established roles in supporting adhesion to and transmigration of lymphocytes across blood vessel endothelium into tissues.
source: These findings are in accord with the well-established roles of LFA1 and ICAM1 in supporting adhesion to and transmigration of lymphocytes across blood vessel endothelium into tissues (Rot and von Andrian, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to established knowledge in the field.

claim: A previous study showed that migration of BM-derived DCs from the SCS into the LN parenchyma was integrin independent.
source: However, they are in discord with a study showing that migration of BM-derived DCs from the SCS into the LN parenchyma was integrin independent (Lämmermann et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Integrins may contribute to DC trafficking into LNs under conditions of inflammation.
source: Moreover, integrins may contribute to DC trafficking into LNs under conditions of inflammation (Teijeira et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: A study of naive lymphocyte egress from LNs showed that LFA1 and ICAM1 can contribute to promoting retention of cells in the LN.
source: A study of naive lymphocyte egress from LNs showed that LFA1 and ICAM1 can contribute to promoting retention of cells in the LN and this was suggested to reflect a role for LFA1 in limiting the rate of cell movement across the endothelium into the sinus lumen (Reichardt et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Following Toxoplasma infection or after vaccinia virus injection, NK cell interaction with CD169+ macrophages is induced.
source: Following Toxoplasma infection or after vaccinia virus injection, NK cell interaction with CD169+ macrophages is induced (Coombes et al., 2012; Garcia et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Previous work showed that innate-like lymphocytes isolated from peripheral LNs were heavily coated with CD169+ macrophage-derived membrane fragments ('blebs').
source: In previous work, we found that innate-like lymphocytes isolated from peripheral LNs were heavily coated with CD169+ macrophage-derived membrane fragments ('blebs') (Gray et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Targeting antigens to CD169 can promote antibody responses.
source: Although CD169 is a defining feature of LN SCS macrophages and targeting antigens to CD169 can promote antibody responses (Macauley et al., 2014), the function of CD169 on these cells is not fully understood.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Crosstalk between sinus-associated macrophages and IFNγ precommitted CD8 T cells and NK cells is important for mounting rapid Th1-like and NK cell responses against acute infection.
source: Crosstalk between sinus-associated macrophages and IFNγ precommitted CD8 T cells and NK cells is important for mounting rapid Th1-like and NK cell responses against acute infection by Pseudomonas aeroguinosa, Salmonella typhimurium and Toxoplasma gondii (Coombes et al., 2012; Kastenmüller et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Our group and others identified populations of innate-like lymphocytes that are enriched near the SCS in peripheral LNs and are pre-committed to produce IL17.
source: In recent work, our group and others identified populations of innate-like (pre-formed effector) lymphocytes that are enriched near the SCS in peripheral LNs and are pre-committed to produce IL17 (Do et al., 2010; Doisne et al., 2009; Gray et al., 2012; Roark et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work by the authors and others.

claim: Within the IL17-committed γδ T cell population, a major subset expresses a Vγ4-containing TCR and undergoes expansion in response to challenge with imiquimod or complete Freund's adjuvant.
source: Within the IL17-committed γδ T cell population a major subset expresses a Vγ4-containing TCR (according to the nomenclature of [Heilig and Tonegawa, 1986]), and undergoes expansion in response to challenge with imiquimod or complete Freund's adjuvant (Gray et al., 2013; Ramirez-Valle et al., 2015; Roark et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: LN DN T cells highly express IL23R and respond to this cytokine.
source: These cells are double negative for CD4 and CD8 (Gray et al., 2012). LN DN T cells highly express IL23R and respond to this cytokine (Mizui et al., 2014; Riol-Blanco et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Innate-like CD8 T cells in LNs rapidly make IFNγ upon cytokine stimulation.
source: These observations are reminiscent of findings for innate-like CD8 T cells in LNs that rapidly make IFNγ upon cytokine (IL18 and IL12 or IL18 and IFNα) stimulation, and for various types of memory T cells that make IFNγ upon IL12 and IL18 exposure (Jameson et al., 2015; Kastenmüller et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Various types of memory T cells make IFNγ upon IL12 and IL18 exposure.
source: These observations are reminiscent of findings for innate-like CD8 T cells in LNs that rapidly make IFNγ upon cytokine (IL18 and IL12 or IL18 and IFNα) stimulation, and for various types of memory T cells that make IFNγ upon IL12 and IL18 exposure (Jameson et al., 2015; Kastenmüller et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The surveillance program of innate-like lymphocytes may allow them to interrogate CD169+ macrophages and SCS for pathogen- or commensal-derived molecules.
source: Although this local migratory behavior was not essential for mounting IL17 responses against the pathogens tested in this study (data not shown), we propose that this surveillance program allows innate like lymphocytes to interrogate the CD169+ macrophages and SCS for pathogen- or commensal-derived molecules for which they have appropriate receptors.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observed migratory behavior.

claim: Within the sinus, cells are exposed to high amounts of S1P that cause rapid, GRK2-dependent internalization and desensitization of S1pr1.
source: Within the sinus, we anticipate that the cells are exposed to high amounts of S1P that cause rapid, GRK2-dependent (Arnon et al., 2011), internalization and desensitization of S1pr1, allowing the cells to respond to cues (possibly including CCL20) that can promote their return to the parenchyma.
evidence: This is an inference based on known S1P biology and the observed cell behavior, with citation to previous work on GRK2-dependent desensitization.

claim: The long ectodomain of CD169 (with 17 Ig-domains) likely contributes to an ability to 'capture' cells that have become dislodged by lymph flow.
source: The long ectodomain of CD169 (with 17 Ig-domains) also seems likely to contribute to an ability to 'capture' cells that have become dislodged by lymph flow and to allow their re-adhesion and subsequent transmigration.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about the structural contribution of CD169 to its function.

claim: A similar activity of CD169 may be involved in capturing CD169-ligand high cells arriving in the SCS from the afferent lymphatic.
source: A similar activity may be involved in capturing CD169-ligand high cells arriving in the SCS from the afferent lymphatic.
evidence: This is a speculative extension of the proposed CD169 function.

claim: The migration of innate-like lymphocytes in close association with SCS macrophages likely ensures that factors made by the macrophages can rapidly engage the lymphocytes.
source: The migration of innate-like lymphocytes in close association with SCS macrophages seems likely to ensure that factors made by the macrophages, such as IL1-family cytokines, can rapidly engage the lymphocytes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed proximity and the demonstrated cytokine-dependent activation.

claim: Cell movement into the lumen of the SCS might allow prompt surveillance of pathogens and endogenous cells arriving via the lymph.
source: The importance of cell movement into the lumen of the SCS is not yet clear but might allow prompt surveillance of pathogens and endogenous cells (e.g. cancer cells) arriving via the lymph, prior to their accessing the LN parenchyma.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional significance of the observed cell movement.

claim: Th17 effector cells that remain in the LN following immunization or infection may position in proximity with the SCS.
source: As well as expression by innate-like lymphocytes, Ccr6 is abundant on Th17 cells (Littman and Rudensky, 2010) and we speculate that Th17 effector cells that remain in the LN following immunization or infection may position in proximity with the SCS.
evidence: This is a speculative extension based on Ccr6 expression on Th17 cells and the demonstrated role of Ccr6 in SCS positioning.

claim: Under inflammatory conditions associated with EAE, CCL20 travels to LNs from the inflamed site and attracts Ccr6+ cells into the sinus lumen.
source: Ccr6 antagonism was suggested to reduce the egress of Ccr6+ effector CD4 T cells from LNs in a mouse EAE model (Liston et al., 2009). CCL20 can be strongly induced in inflamed tissue (Mabuchi et al., 2013), and we speculate that under the inflammatory condition associated with EAE, CCL20 travels to LNs from the inflamed site and attracts Ccr6+ cells into the sinus lumen as we observed following CCL20 injection.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of previous findings in the context of the current study's results.
